screens.title: Restore options and workflows
screens.narratorSegment: mongorestore reads BSON files produced by mongodump and writes them back into a running mongod instance. It can restore entire backup directories, a single database, or an individual collection. By default, mongorestore inserts documents; it does not replace existing collections unless you use options like --drop. The --upsert option provides an alternative behavior where existing documents that match on _id are updated rather than duplicated. For routine restores, many teams restore into a standalone mongod instance, validate the data, and then return the server to a replica set so it can catch up. This minimizes the risk of conflicting writes during restore. Remember that mongorestore may take time to rebuild indexes after inserting data; consider using --noIndexRestore during initial data load and rebuild indexes later to improve throughput. A common misconception is that mongorestore will automatically replace existing data; without --drop or careful use of --upsert, you may end up with duplicate documents or conflicting states. As a practical example, to restore a single collection you point mongorestore at the collection BSON file and pass --db and --collection flags. The core insight is to plan whether you need a destructive replace or an idempotent upsert, and to choose flags that match that plan.

keyIdea.title: Choose flags to match intent
keyIdea.text: Decide before you restore whether to drop and replace, upsert, or skip index restoration to control behavior and performance.

content.html:
Core Concept Restore options and workflows
mongorestore behaviors and flags
Understand insertion, dropping, upsert behavior and index handling.
Definition and common flags
--drop drops the target collection before restoring, ensuring an exact replacement.
--upsert updates existing documents that match on _id instead of inserting duplicates.
--noIndexRestore skips restoring indexes so you can rebuild them later for performance.
--oplogReplay applies oplog entries during restore for point-in-time recovery (requires oplog files).
Key Takeaway

Pick flags that reflect whether you want destructive replace, incremental updates, or faster index handling.

Concrete example
# Restore a specific collection, dropping it first
mongorestore --port 27017 --db mydatabase --collection users --drop /data/backups/mydatabase/users.bson

# Restore but skip index restoration for faster load
mongorestore --port 27017 --db mydatabase --noIndexRestore /data/backups/mydatabase
Misconception
mongorestore does not implicitly overwrite existing documents. Unless you use --drop or --upsert, you can leave duplicate or conflicting data in place.

screens.title: Practical mongorestore examples
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s walk through concrete mongorestore commands you will run in a lab. Restoring an entire backup directory is the simplest case: point mongorestore at the backup folder and it will iterate databases and collections that mongodump created. For example, running mongorestore against /data/backups/mydatabase_backup restores all contents into the running mongod. If you only need one database, use --db and specify the path to that database folder. For a single collection, supply both --db and --collection and point to the users. bson file. Note that when restoring to a production system you must plan index rebuild time. You can use --noIndexRestore to load data quickly and then recreate indexes during a maintenance window. Another practical pattern is to restore into a temporary standalone mongod, connect with the shell to run verification queries, and then promote or rejoin the node to the replica set. A common trap is forgetting to escape filenames or presuming mongorestore will correct permissions: ensure the mongod process has file system access to the backup files if you use file-based restore flows. In the example code panels you can copy the exact calls used in the lab activity.

keyIdea.title: Commands you can run
keyIdea.text: Use mongorestore with directory, db, or collection targets and plan index rebuild time or use --noIndexRestore to speed initial loads.

content.html:
Process Flow Practical mongorestore examples
Terminal-style command examples for practice
Restore entire backup directory
mongorestore --port 27017 /data/backups/mydatabase_backup
This restores all databases and collections that exist in the backup directory.
Restore a single database
mongorestore --port 27017 --db mydatabase /data/backups/mydatabase_backup/mydatabase
Use this to restore only one logical database from a larger dump set.
Restore a single collection
mongorestore --port 27017 --db mydatabase --collection users /data/backups/mydatabase_backup/mydatabase/users.bson
Good for surgical recovery when only one collection was lost or damaged.
Restore with drop
mongorestore --port 27017 --db testdb --collection sampledata --drop /tmp/mongo_backup/testdb_backup/testdb/sampledata.bson
Use when you want an exact replacement of the collection contents from the backup.

screens.title: Restoring into replica sets
screens.narratorSegment: Replica sets require deliberate handling when restoring data. The safest pattern for many DBAs is to restore a backup onto a standalone mongod instance first. Once the data is validated, add the node back into the replica set as a new member so it can replicate from the primary and catch up. This avoids writing directly to a member that is already part of a set and causing potential conflicts. Alternatively, you can restore directly to the primary, but you must be aware of the consequences: restored data might conflict with recent writes on secondaries, and indexes may be rebuilt while the primary is serving traffic. If you choose to restore to a member already in the set, consider removing it temporarily from the set or stopping replication on that member until the restore completes. After a restore, check the replication state and initial sync progress, and watch for rollback events. A common misconception is that restoring a member will automatically reconcile divergent histories; in reality, mismatches can trigger rollbacks or require a full resync. Plan for index rebuild time and monitor replication lag until the cluster is fully healthy again. The key takeaway is to favor restoring into an isolated instance and then reintroducing it to the replica set after verification.

keyIdea.title: Restore to isolated node first
keyIdea.text: Restore to a standalone node, verify data, then rejoin the replica set so replication can resume cleanly.

content.html:
Definition Restoring into replica sets
Recommended workflow
  1. Restore backup into a standalone mongod instance.
  2. Run integrity checks and application-level queries to validate data.
  3. Stop mongod, join it to the replica set as a new member, allow initial sync.
  4. Monitor replication lag and health until the member is fully caught up.
Pitfalls and checks
  • Restoring to an existing member without isolation may cause conflicts or rollbacks.
  • Indexes rebuild time can prolong catch-up; account for this in maintenance windows.
  • Verify oplog size and window if you plan to use oplog-driven PITR after restore.
Pro tip: preserve the original node’s replica set configuration and tags if rejoining to avoid unwanted election behavior.

screens.title: Restoring in sharded clusters
screens.narratorSegment: Sharded clusters add coordination requirements to restores. A full restore for a sharded deployment often requires restoring config servers first, then restoring data on each shard, and finally bringing the cluster back online and restarting the balancer. Because data is distributed across shards, restoring with mongorestore against a mongos will route documents to proper shards, but restoring an entire sharded cluster from mongodump files often demands careful sequencing. For example, you may need to stop the balancer during restore to prevent chunk migrations and potential inconsistencies. Another pattern is to restore each shard independently and then ensure the cluster metadata in the config servers matches the restored data. The misconception here is assuming a single mongorestore invocation will preserve the exact sharded topology without additional coordination. Also consider index definitions: each shard requires its local indexes restored, and restoring large shards can take substantial time and disk space. If you use filesystem snapshots for shards, ensure snapshots are coordinated or that shard-level restores are performed in a controlled order. Plan maintenance windows, disable automatic balancing where needed, and validate chunk placement and config server state after the restore completes.

keyIdea.text: Sharded clusters require ordering, balancer control, and careful verification of config servers and shards after restoring.

content.html:
Comparison Restoring in sharded clusters
Key steps for shard restores
  • Stop the balancer to prevent migrations during restore.
  • Restore config servers first to ensure correct metadata.
  • Restore each shard’s data and indexes, then reattach shards if necessary.
  • Restart the balancer after verifying cluster consistency.
Operational notes
Sharded restores often need coordination across teams because they touch routing metadata and many nodes. Ensure you have a rollback plan if chunk mapping mismatches appear, and test restores in a staging environment before attempting production restores.

screens.title: Filesystem snapshot restores
screens.narratorSegment: Filesystem snapshots capture the entire data directory at block level and can be a fast way to restore full mongod instances. To ensure snapshot consistency, you typically issue an fsyncLock on the mongod instance before taking the snapshot. fsyncLock flushes all writes to disk and prevents further writes, which gives you a consistent on-disk state. After the snapshot completes, release the lock and resume normal operation. When you need to restore, revert the block device to the snapshot state and restart mongod. For replica set members, the restored node will normally rejoin the set and resync as needed. For standalone instances, a restart should bring the data back as-of the snapshot moment. A common failure after a filesystem restore is incorrect file permissions or ownership; ensure the mongod process user owns the data files and that file permissions allow read and write access. Another practical consideration is disk space: restoring a large snapshot may require temporary space for journals or index rebuilds. Finally, snapshots taken without fsyncLock can result in an inconsistent database state leading to repair steps or data loss; always prefer a locked snapshot for production restores.

keyIdea.text: Lock the database during the snapshot to ensure on-disk consistency, then verify permissions and disk space after restore.

content.html:
Process Flow Filesystem snapshot restores
Snapshot sequence
  1. Issue fsyncLock to flush and pause writes.
  2. Take the block-level snapshot of the disk.
  3. Release fsyncLock to resume writes.
  4. When needed, revert the block device to the snapshot and start mongod.
Checklist after restore
  • Fix file ownership and permissions for the mongod user.
  • Ensure sufficient disk space for journals and indexes.
  • Monitor mongod logs for any recovery or repair steps required.

screens.title: Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)
screens.narratorSegment: Point-in-time recovery gives you the ability to restore the database to an exact second in the past. The technique combines a base backup — typically a filesystem snapshot or mongodump taken before the desired recovery point — and a stream of oplog entries recorded after that backup. The oplog is a capped collection that records all write operations on a replica set. To perform PITR, you first restore the base backup to the node. Then you replay oplog entries from the time of the backup up to the target timestamp. In practice, mongorestore supports an --oplogReplay option that can apply oplog entries during restore when provided with appropriate oplog files. Tools like Cloud Manager and Ops Manager automate oplog collection and replay, reducing manual complexity. When doing manual PITR, you must ensure your oplog chain is complete: any gap between the base backup and the desired point will prevent exact reconstruction. A common misconception is that PITR is trivial with a backup alone; without a continuous oplog history the restore can only reach the snapshot time. The important operational lesson is to retain oplog segments long enough to cover your desired recovery window and to test oplog replay in non-production environments before relying on it.

keyIdea.title: PITR needs oplog continuity
keyIdea.text: A base backup plus an unbroken oplog chain is required to reach a specific point-in-time during recovery.

content.html:
Core Concept Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)
PITR steps
  1. Restore a base backup taken before your target time.
  2. Collect oplog entries from after the backup time up to the desired timestamp.
  3. Apply the oplog entries to roll the database forward to the target time.
Practical cautions
Ensure no gaps in oplog retention. Test oplog replay in a staging environment. Consider automated tools to capture and store oplog streams continuously.

screens.title: Applying oplog replay
screens.narratorSegment: Applying oplog entries requires careful handling of the oplog files and the correct restore sequence. First, ensure you have a base backup that corresponds to an earlier oplog position. When you use mongorestore with --oplogReplay, you supply the oplog. bson file that contains the sequence of operations to be applied. mongorestore will apply the oplog entries in order, effectively rolling the database forward. Pay attention to timestamps and ordering: oplog entries must be continuous and complete from the backup time to the desired recovery time. If any oplog segment is missing or corrupted, you will be unable to reconstruct the intermediate state and must either choose an earlier recovery point or accept partial recovery. Another practical issue is conflict handling: oplog replay re-applies operations as they originally occurred; if the restored data differs in unexpected ways, replay may fail or produce inconsistent results. Always validate the final state by running integrity checks and application-level tests. Because manual oplog replay can be complex, many teams use automated tools that stream and store oplog entries for reliable PITR. The essential point is that oplog replay is powerful but fragile — it requires complete, ordered data and careful validation after the operation.

keyIdea.title: Oplog replay needs ordered, complete data
keyIdea.text: Ensure you have a continuous chain of oplog entries from your backup to the desired timestamp before attempting replay.

content.html:
Process Flow Applying oplog replay
Example command
# After restoring base backup
mongorestore --port 27017 --oplogReplay --oplogFile /data/backups/oplog.bson /data/backups/base_backup
mongorestore will apply oplog entries in order to move the data forward from the snapshot time.
Checks before replay
  • Confirm oplog coverage from backup start to target time.
  • Validate file integrity and sequence numbers of oplog segments.
  • Test replay in staging when possible to ensure no unexpected conflicts.

screens.title: Common mistakes during restore
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring issues surface during restores. First, file system permissions and ownership are a frequent cause of mongod failing to start after a filesystem restore. If the restored files are owned by the user who performed the copy rather than the mongod user, the server cannot access its data. Always chown and set correct permissions before starting mongod. Second, disk space can be underestimated: during restore, temporary space may be required for journals, index builds, or staged files. Monitor available capacity and plan ahead. Third, index rebuilding can significantly increase restore time. You can speed initial data load by using --noIndexRestore and then creating indexes afterwards, but ensure you have a maintenance window for index creation. Fourth, oplog gaps will prevent point-in-time recovery; retention policies must be configured to keep oplog entries long enough for your recovery window. Lastly, in sharded clusters failing to stop the balancer can cause migration churn during restore. A common misconception is that restores are purely file operations; they are also cluster and topology operations that require coordination, validation, and post-restore checks. The practical advice is to run test restores, script your steps, and include verification queries to confirm application-level assumptions after a restore.

Hands-on Activity Restore a collection with --drop
Task steps
  1. Add distinct documents to testdb.sampledata to test drop behavior.
  2. Run mongorestore with --db, --collection, and --drop against the sampledata.bson file.
  3. Connect via the shell and verify collection contents match the backup.
Starter command
mongorestore --port 27017 --db testdb --collection sampledata --drop /tmp/mongo_backup/testdb_backup/testdb/sampledata.bson
Verify by running db.sampledata.find().pretty() in mongosh after the restore.

screens.title: Verification and post-restore checks
screens.narratorSegment: Validation after a restore prevents surprises. First, run basic sanity queries: counts per collection, sample documents, and checksum comparisons if available. Check indexes exist and are usable; missing or incomplete indexes can change query plans and degrade application performance. Inspect mongod logs for repair or recovery messages that indicate internal correction steps ran during startup. For replica sets, verify replication status and ensure that no members are in a recovering or rollback state. For sharded clusters, confirm config server status and chunk distribution and run a few application-level tests to ensure routing works as expected. A useful verification step is to run the same test suite you use during deployments against the restored dataset to detect schema or data anomalies. Pay special attention to timestamps and timezones if you use date-based queries in your application; restores from different snapshots can surface subtle differences. Finally, document the post-restore state: counts, indexes, and any error messages. This record shortens recovery time in future incidents and helps refine your runbook. Remember: a successful restore is not only about files restored but about the application behaving correctly after the operation.

fullNarratorScript:
Restoring data is where backups prove their value. In this lesson you will learn practical, repeatable ways to recover MongoDB data from mongodump archives, from filesystem snapshots, and by using the oplog for point-in-time recovery. You will see the exact commands for mongorestore, the role of options like --drop and --oplogReplay, and how to think about restores inside replica sets and sharded clusters. We’ll also cover filesystem-snapshot restores and why fsyncLock matters. Finally, you’ll learn common troubleshooting steps — checking permissions, confirming disk space, and validating data after a restore. Each topic includes a concrete example you can practice in a lab, and a short checklist to help you avoid the most frequent mistakes. By the end of this chapter you should be able to choose the right restore path, run mongorestore with appropriate flags, plan a PITR workflow with oplog replay, and verify the integrity of the recovered data. Ask yourself: after a restore, how will you validate that your application’s assumptions still hold?

By the end of these lessons you will be able to run mongorestore to import BSON backups, choose the correct restore path for replica sets and sharded clusters, and plan point-in-time recovery using the oplog. You’ll practice restoring an entire backup, restoring a single database or collection, and using the --drop option safely. You will also understand filesystem snapshot restores: how fsyncLock creates a consistent snapshot, and how to restore and restart mongod after reverting a block device. Finally, you will learn the operational checks to perform after every restore — file permissions, disk space, and application-level data validation. Each objective focuses on practical steps and checks so that restores are repeatable and auditable. Practicing these skills in a lab ensures you can react to corruption or accidental deletion with confidence. Which objective matters most depends on your environment, but all four contribute to a robust recovery practice.

These objectives emphasize hands-on practice: you will restore an individual collection using mongorestore with --drop, verify the restored documents using a shell, and inspect startup logs if a filesystem restore fails. Practicing restores in a controlled lab helps you discover practical issues: ownership and permission mismatches, insufficient disk space, and index rebuilding time. You will also plan a simple PITR sequence: take a base snapshot, retain oplog entries, and practice replaying the oplog up to a chosen timestamp. Finally, you will learn site-specific considerations for replica sets and sharded clusters so you can coordinate restores without causing split-brain or data divergence. Regularly exercising these tasks reduces recovery time and gives you confidence during real incidents. After hands-on practice, you should be able to document the restore steps for your environment and run them under time pressure.

mongorestore reads BSON files produced by mongodump and writes them back into a running mongod instance. It can restore entire backup directories, a single database, or an individual collection. By default, mongorestore inserts documents; it does not replace existing collections unless you use options like --drop. The --upsert option provides an alternative behavior where existing documents that match on _id are updated rather than duplicated. For routine restores, many teams restore into a standalone mongod instance, validate the data, and then return the server to a replica set so it can catch up. This minimizes the risk of conflicting writes during restore. Remember that mongorestore may take time to rebuild indexes after inserting data; consider using --noIndexRestore during initial data load and rebuild indexes later to improve throughput. A common misconception is that mongorestore will automatically replace existing data; without --drop or careful use of --upsert, you may end up with duplicate documents or conflicting states. As a practical example, to restore a single collection you point mongorestore at the collection BSON file and pass --db and --collection flags. The core insight is to plan whether you need a destructive replace or an idempotent upsert, and to choose flags that match that plan.

Let’s walk through concrete mongorestore commands you will run in a lab. Restoring an entire backup directory is the simplest case: point mongorestore at the backup folder and it will iterate databases and collections that mongodump created. For example, running mongorestore against /data/backups/mydatabase_backup restores all contents into the running mongod. If you only need one database, use --db and specify the path to that database folder. For a single collection, supply both --db and --collection and point to the users. bson file. Note that when restoring to a production system you must plan index rebuild time. You can use --noIndexRestore to load data quickly and then recreate indexes during a maintenance window. Another practical pattern is to restore into a temporary standalone mongod, connect with the shell to run verification queries, and then promote or rejoin the node to the replica set. A common trap is forgetting to escape filenames or presuming mongorestore will correct permissions: ensure the mongod process has file system access to the backup files if you use file-based restore flows. In the example code panels you can copy the exact calls used in the lab activity.

Replica sets require deliberate handling when restoring data. The safest pattern for many DBAs is to restore a backup onto a standalone mongod instance first. Once the data is validated, add the node back into the replica set as a new member so it can replicate from the primary and catch up. This avoids writing directly to a member that is already part of a set and causing potential conflicts. Alternatively, you can restore directly to the primary, but you must be aware of the consequences: restored data might conflict with recent writes on secondaries, and indexes may be rebuilt while the primary is serving traffic. If you choose to restore to a member already in the set, consider removing it temporarily from the set or stopping replication on that member until the restore completes. After a restore, check the replication state and initial sync progress, and watch for rollback events. A common misconception is that restoring a member will automatically reconcile divergent histories; in reality, mismatches can trigger rollbacks or require a full resync. Plan for index rebuild time and monitor replication lag until the cluster is fully healthy again. The key takeaway is to favor restoring into an isolated instance and then reintroducing it to the replica set after verification.

Sharded clusters add coordination requirements to restores. A full restore for a sharded deployment often requires restoring config servers first, then restoring data on each shard, and finally bringing the cluster back online and restarting the balancer. Because data is distributed across shards, restoring with mongorestore against a mongos will route documents to proper shards, but restoring an entire sharded cluster from mongodump files often demands careful sequencing. For example, you may need to stop the balancer during restore to prevent chunk migrations and potential inconsistencies. Another pattern is to restore each shard independently and then ensure the cluster metadata in the config servers matches the restored data. The misconception here is assuming a single mongorestore invocation will preserve the exact sharded topology without additional coordination. Also consider index definitions: each shard requires its local indexes restored, and restoring large shards can take substantial time and disk space. If you use filesystem snapshots for shards, ensure snapshots are coordinated or that shard-level restores are performed in a controlled order. Plan maintenance windows, disable automatic balancing where needed, and validate chunk placement and config server state after the restore completes.

Filesystem snapshots capture the entire data directory at block level and can be a fast way to restore full mongod instances. To ensure snapshot consistency, you typically issue an fsyncLock on the mongod instance before taking the snapshot. fsyncLock flushes all writes to disk and prevents further writes, which gives you a consistent on-disk state. After the snapshot completes, release the lock and resume normal operation. When you need to restore, revert the block device to the snapshot state and restart mongod. For replica set members, the restored node will normally rejoin the set and resync as needed. For standalone instances, a restart should bring the data back as-of the snapshot moment. A common failure after a filesystem restore is incorrect file permissions or ownership; ensure the mongod process user owns the data files and that file permissions allow read and write access. Another practical consideration is disk space: restoring a large snapshot may require temporary space for journals or index rebuilds. Finally, snapshots taken without fsyncLock can result in an inconsistent database state leading to repair steps or data loss; always prefer a locked snapshot for production restores.

Point-in-time recovery gives you the ability to restore the database to an exact second in the past. The technique combines a base backup — typically a filesystem snapshot or mongodump taken before the desired recovery point — and a stream of oplog entries recorded after that backup. The oplog is a capped collection that records all write operations on a replica set. To perform PITR, you first restore the base backup to the node. Then you replay oplog entries from the time of the backup up to the target timestamp. In practice, mongorestore supports an --oplogReplay option that can apply oplog entries during restore when provided with appropriate oplog files. Tools like Cloud Manager and Ops Manager automate oplog collection and replay, reducing manual complexity. When doing manual PITR, you must ensure your oplog chain is complete: any gap between the base backup and the desired point will prevent exact reconstruction. A common misconception is that PITR is trivial with a backup alone; without a continuous oplog history the restore can only reach the snapshot time. The important operational lesson is to retain oplog segments long enough to cover your desired recovery window and to test oplog replay in non-production environments before relying on it.

Applying oplog entries requires careful handling of the oplog files and the correct restore sequence. First, ensure you have a base backup that corresponds to an earlier oplog position. When you use mongorestore with --oplogReplay, you supply the oplog. bson file that contains the sequence of operations to be applied. mongorestore will apply the oplog entries in order, effectively rolling the database forward. Pay attention to timestamps and ordering: oplog entries must be continuous and complete from the backup time to the desired recovery time. If any oplog segment is missing or corrupted, you will be unable to reconstruct the intermediate state and must either choose an earlier recovery point or accept partial recovery. Another practical issue is conflict handling: oplog replay re-applies operations as they originally occurred; if the restored data differs in unexpected ways, replay may fail or produce inconsistent results. Always validate the final state by running integrity checks and application-level tests. Because manual oplog replay can be complex, many teams use automated tools that stream and store oplog entries for reliable PITR. The essential point is that oplog replay is powerful but fragile — it requires complete, ordered data and careful validation after the operation.
